result: The Drosophila larval visual system consists of simple eyes (Bolwig Organ) with approximately 12 photoreceptor neurons per eye, comprising two subtypes (Rh5 and Rh6) with distinct spectral sensitivities and behavioral roles. These photoreceptors project via the Bolwig nerve to the larval optic neuropil (LON) and mediate diverse behaviors including navigation, circadian entrainment, and associative memory.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are well-supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing the basic anatomy and function of the larval visual system. The claims accurately describe established knowledge about photoreceptor number, rhodopsin expression, spectral tuning, and behavioral roles, providing essential background context for the study.

result: Previous studies identified eleven neurons innervating the LON per hemisphere, including lateral neurons, optic lobe pioneer cells, and a serotonergic neuron, plus two unpaired octopaminergic/tyraminergic neurons. Prior EM work showed that photoreceptor axons form polyadic synapses and target OLPs.
evaluation: Claims C8-C11 accurately summarize prior anatomical and connectomic findings from cited literature, establishing the baseline knowledge that motivated the current comprehensive reconstruction. These claims provide appropriate context for the novelty of the complete circuit mapping presented in this study.

result: The authors reconstructed the complete synaptic wiring diagram of the LON from a whole first instar larval CNS ssTEM volume, identifying 60 neurons (11 second-order interneurons, 2 third-order interneurons, 1 serotonergic neuron per hemisphere, plus 2 unpaired octopaminergic/tyraminergic neurons) with 12.5 mm of cable, 2090 presynaptic sites, and 4414 postsynaptic sites. The reconstruction required 134 hours plus 43 hours of proofreading.
evaluation: Claims C12-C14, C20, C86-C87 describe the core methodological achievement and quantitative results of the reconstruction. The use of an established ssTEM dataset (Ohyama et al., 2015) and CATMAID reconstruction tools is well-documented. The neuron counts, cable length, synapse counts, and reconstruction time provide concrete metrics of the work performed and are internally consistent.

result: Neurotransmitter identity was determined for LON neurons: one lOLP is cholinergic (cha-lOLP) and the other glutamatergic (glu-lOLP); all VPNs except the peptidergic Pdf-LaNs are cholinergic; and the VPLN is glutamatergic.
evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and are consistent with prior literature (Yasuyama et al., 1995; Daniels et al., 2008). The neurotransmitter assignments are critical for functional interpretation of the circuit and appear well-validated through multiple approaches.

result: The LON is organized into three distinct layers based on photoreceptor innervation: Rh6-PRs terminate in the distal layer (LONd), Rh5-PRs in the intermediate layer (LONi), and the proximal layer (LONp) lacks direct photoreceptor input.
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 describe the layered organization of the LON, supported by both the current EM reconstruction data (Figure 2A-C) and prior work (Sprecher et al., 2011). The stratification is a key organizational principle that parallels other visual systems and is clearly demonstrated in the 3D reconstructions.

result: Most VPNs receive direct inputs only from Rh5-PRs, while Pdf-LaNs uniquely integrate inputs from both Rh5- and Rh6-PRs by spanning both LONd and LONi. Third-order interneurons (VPLN and Tiny VLN) in the LONp receive no direct photoreceptor input.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are directly supported by the connectivity data shown in Figures 1E-K, 2E, and 3B. The differential connectivity patterns are quantified in the connectivity matrices and are central to understanding how the two photoreceptor pathways are segregated and integrated within the circuit.

result: VPNs project to three protocerebral areas (superior lateral, lateral inferior, and ventro lateral protocerebrum) that overlap with the lateral horn and mushroom body calyx. Within the LON, VPN dendrites are mainly postsynaptic, while their axons in higher brain areas have both pre- and postsynaptic sites, suggesting modulation by non-visual inputs. pOLP and VPLN receive up to 30% of inputs from non-LON neurons.
evaluation: Claims C31-C36 describe VPN projection patterns and synaptic polarity, supported by Figures 1E-K, 2C-E, and comparison with the olfactory system (Berck et al., 2016). The observation of mixed pre/postsynaptic sites on VPN axons and significant non-LON inputs is well-documented in the data and suggests functional parallels with other sensory systems.

result: Rh6-PRs synapse primarily onto VLNs (79%) with minimal VPN input (15%, exclusively to Pdf-LaNs), while Rh5-PRs preferentially target VPNs (90%) with minimal VLN input (6%). Pdf-LaNs are the only interneurons receiving direct inputs from both photoreceptor subtypes.
evaluation: Claims C37-C39 quantify the segregation of photoreceptor pathways, supported by connectivity data in Figure 2E and source data. The percentages are precise and demonstrate clear pathway separation, with Pdf-LaNs as the exception. This finding is consistent with behavioral evidence that either PR subtype can entrain the circadian clock (Keene et al., 2011).

result: The two lOLPs receive the majority of their inputs from Rh6-PRs (75% for cha-lOLP, 58% for glu-lOLP) and synapse onto most VPNs. pOLP is the only VPN not receiving lOLP input, creating a direct Rh5-PR output pathway. pOLP and PVL09 are strongly interconnected through axo-axonic connections.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 detail the connectivity of lOLPs and their role in relaying Rh6-PR information to VPNs, supported by Figures 2E-F, 3A-C, and source data. The identification of pOLP as receiving only direct Rh5-PR input and its reciprocal connection with PVL09 are important circuit features clearly demonstrated in the connectivity matrices.

result: The third-order interneuron VPLN receives no direct photoreceptor input but is downstream of both lOLPs and connects to multiple VPNs (5th-LaN, nc-LaNs, PVL09), creating an additional computational layer.
evaluation: Claims C44-C45 describe the VPLN as a third-order neuron in the circuit hierarchy, supported by Figures 3B-E. The VPLN's position in the circuit and its connectivity pattern suggest it may play a role in temporal processing of visual information, as discussed in the manuscript.

result: VPNs target distinct higher brain regions: pOLP projects to the lower lateral horn (overlapping with olfactory mPN Seahorse); three VPNs (5th-LaN, nc-LaN 1 and 2) project to both lateral horn and mushroom body calyx, synapsing onto Kenyon cells; PVL09 has a bifurcated axon projecting to lateral horn and looping below the mushroom body.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 describe VPN projection patterns to higher brain centers, supported by Figures 1E-J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and citations (Berck et al., 2016; Eichler et al., 2017). The anatomical descriptions are detailed and consistent with known brain anatomy. The overlap with olfactory and memory centers suggests functional roles in innate and learned behaviors.

result: Pdf-LaNs project dorsally and medially to the lateral horn, making small dyadic synapses from boutons containing dense-core vesicles and clear vesicles, suggesting co-expression of Pdf neuropeptide and possibly glycine as a neurotransmitter.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 describe Pdf-LaN anatomy and vesicle content, supported by Figures 1G, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 3, EM images, and citations (Yasuyama and Meinertzhagen, 2010; Frenkel et al., 2017). The observation of both dense-core and clear vesicles is consistent with peptidergic neurons that may co-release classical neurotransmitters.

result: Aminergic modulatory neurons provide feedback to the LON: serotonergic SP2-1 neurons connect contralaterally to lOLPs and VPLN; octopaminergic/tyraminergic sVUM2 neurons innervate both hemispheres symmetrically, synapsing onto lOLPs, which form feedback synapses onto sVUM2 axon terminals.
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 describe modulatory inputs to the LON, supported by Figures 4A-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The contralateral serotonergic projection and bilateral octopaminergic innervation are clearly demonstrated. The feedback from lOLPs to sVUM2 (but not SP2-1) suggests differential regulation of these modulatory systems.

result: The specimen shows variable photoreceptor numbers (13 PRs in left hemisphere, 16 in right) and an additional third lOLP in the right hemisphere. Despite these numerical differences, homologous interneurons receive similar fractions of photoreceptor inputs in both hemispheres.
evaluation: Claims C58-C62 document biological variability in cell numbers while demonstrating circuit robustness, supported by the reconstruction data and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The observation that interneurons maintain proportional connectivity despite variable PR numbers is important and parallels findings in the olfactory system (Tobin et al., 2017).

result: Spectral graph analysis shows that despite left and right LONs having different numbers of PRs and lOLPs and sharing no interneurons, neurons of the same type cluster closely together, indicating similar circuit structure. The overall circuit architecture and output channels (VPNs) are maintained despite numerical variability.
evaluation: Claims C63-C64 present quantitative analysis of circuit similarity across hemispheres using spectral graph methods, supported by Figure 5A. This analysis demonstrates that circuit topology is preserved despite cell number variability, an important finding for understanding developmental robustness and circuit function.

result: The two photoreceptor subtypes connect to distinct interneuron subsets, showing separation of light signal flow at the first synapse. Network analysis suggests the resulting circuits may encode both ambient light intensity and changes in light intensity.
evaluation: Claim C15 is well-supported by connectivity data showing clear pathway segregation. However, C16's functional interpretation about encoding ambient vs. changing light intensity is speculative, based on network topology rather than physiological recordings. While the circuit architecture is consistent with this hypothesis, direct experimental validation of these proposed functions is needed.

result: The stratified structure of the larval optic neuropil suggests common organizational principles with adult fly and vertebrate visual systems.
evaluation: Claim C17 is supported by the demonstrated layered organization of the LON and detailed comparisons with adult fly and vertebrate visual systems presented in Figure 6 and the Discussion. The parallel between LON layers and lamina/medulla in flies or retinal layers in vertebrates represents a meaningful comparative insight.

result: Larval photoreceptors lack rhabdomeric structure, intracellular pigment granules, and the Bolwig organ lacks focusing optics, yet larval PRs express the main phototransduction pathway components like adult PRs.
evaluation: Claims C65-C68 accurately summarize established anatomical and molecular differences and similarities between larval and adult photoreceptors, supported by multiple citations (Green et al., 1993; Sprecher et al., 2007; Rosenbaum et al., 2011; Mishra et al., 2016; Bernardo-Garcia et al., 2016). This provides important context for interpreting larval visual function.

result: In the larval visual circuit, there are no significant synaptic connections onto photoreceptors, suggesting light information is passed on without alteration at the first synapse level.
evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by connectivity data in Figures 2E and 5B showing minimal feedback to PRs. This contrasts with other sensory systems (olfactory, mechanosensory) where presynaptic inhibition is common, and represents an important circuit feature. The interpretation that information passes unaltered is reasonable given the lack of feedback.

result: Comparisons with adult fly visual system and olfactory system reveal shared organizational features including neurotransmitter usage, layered organization, and circuit motifs, while highlighting key differences such as the reciprocal connections between larval lOLPs and the cholinergic nature of larval PRs.
evaluation: Claims C70-C82 present comparative analyses with adult visual and larval olfactory systems, supported by extensive citations and the authors' own data. These comparisons are well-reasoned and identify both conserved principles (layering, neurotransmitter types, modulatory inputs) and system-specific features (PR neurotransmitters, lOLP interconnections). The comparisons provide valuable context for interpreting larval circuit function.

result: Functional parallels between visual and olfactory circuits include reciprocal motifs that may compute stimulus derivatives, projection interneurons conveying mixed intensity and temporal information, and feedback connections from local interneurons to octopaminergic/tyraminergic modulatory neurons.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 propose functional interpretations based on circuit similarities with the olfactory system (Berck et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015). While the structural parallels are well-documented, the functional interpretations remain hypothetical without physiological validation. The comparisons are reasonable and generate testable hypotheses, but the proposed functions are inferred rather than demonstrated.
